extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / scientists / Royal Society readers
extracted.subtask_description: A 17th-century scientific discourse on the weight, elasticity, and variable gravity of the air and how these properties explain vapour behaviour, rain, winds, barometer readings, and related meteorological phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of auroral/sky phenomena with high barometer
rubrics_metrics.description: Northern lights (caprae saltantes) and certain great lights are often observed when the mercury has been high in the barometer and appear in the quarter of the heavens where the sun is then below the horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjecture that vapours may have ascended beyond the earth's shadow and by refracting beams of light occasion these lights; also consider whether red evening skies (which denote fair weather) proceed from the height of the clouds occasioned by increased specific gravity of the atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapour ascent and descent linked to air's specific gravity (barometer behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vapours ascend when their gravity is less than that of the surrounding air and fall (forming clouds, fogs, rain, snow) usually when the mercury subsides a little and the atmosphere's gravity is lessened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'constant observation' of barometer watchers: subsidence of mercury often precedes gathering of clouds and precipitation. Use barometric trend as an indicator of vapour behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rain during rising mercury explained by wind-driven coalescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rain observed while the mercury is rising can occur when winds have carried clouds toward one quarter and a sudden change of wind drives formerly scattered vapours together into little drops which then fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take rain during rising mercury as a refutation of barometric- vapour theory; instead check for recent wind changes that could have caused mechanical coalescence of droplets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winds arise from local differences in air pressure/weight (Archimedean principle applied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the notion that parts less pressed give way to those more pressed, if the air becomes specifically lighter in one place, neighbouring heavier parts run thither in a current until equilibrium is restored — producing winds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider spatial and temporal non-uniformity of air gravity (barometer readings differ by place/time); wind strength and duration depend on the portion of air thus changed and the degree of weight/spring differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical link: barometer motion frequently accompanies wind onset
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the mercury is often found to subside for the most part in the barometer at the rising of winds; the barometer is in motion (rising or falling) when winds begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use barometer variability (not just absolute height) as corroborating evidence for changing atmospheric pressure associated with winds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible causes of changes in air's specific gravity — subtile fluid hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulate of a fluid much more subtile than common air and of far greater pressure that causes continuity/cohesion of bodies and in which the air 'floats' — such a body's nature might influence changes in the air's gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer as a speculative hypothesis; no cogent experiments given to prove its weight or elasticity. Treat as an avenue for future inquiry rather than established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible causes: chemical infusion altering air's specific gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy to infusion of one liquor into another altering specific gravity (e.g., aqua regis and gold particles) suggests that plenty of nitrous steams or similar mixtures in the air may alter its specific gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider chemical composition of atmosphere (presence of vapours, steams) as a factor in barometric/meteorological changes; this is presented as a speculative chemical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature (heat/cold) influences the air's spring and thus its effective weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of the air's spring (elasticity) diminishes its weight (rarefaction); lessening of its spring increases its weight (condensation). For example, cold weather and sharp frosts often show higher mercury in the barometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat thermal effects on elasticity and specific gravity as central: heating rarefies and weakens intensive gravity; cooling condenses and intensifies gravity. Use seasonal/temperature correlations (e.g., north winds cause higher mercury) to test this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal/solar-position effect on rainfall via rarefaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries near the line (tropics) have continual rains when the sun is nearest (their 'winter') possibly because extraordinary rarefaction and lessening of specific gravity there draw vapours and cause floods of rain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use solar declination/seasonal position as explanatory factor for regional differences in precipitation; this links solar heating and atmospheric rarefaction to large-scale rainfall patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of wind direction with barometer readings (north vs south winds)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the wind is north, north-east, or north-west the mercury ever rises (air heavier); when the wind is from the south, south-east, or south-west it falls (air lighter). Cold winds fill sails more forcibly than warm winds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prevailing wind direction as an empirical predictor of barometric tendency and air weight; this is an observational rule of thumb for the region discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative gravity of vapours demonstrated by Boyle experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Boyle's distillation of a blood-red liquor: when the phial is stopped no smoke appears; when unstopped and external air admitted a copious white smoke rises; in a receiver (vacuum) the liquor does not emit visible steams — showing that vapours ascend only when the ambient air's gravity is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled pump-out experiments to compare vapour behaviour under reduced air gravity vs ordinary air; vapour ascent depends on relative gravity of vapour vs ambient air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere behaves as heterogeneous mixture with parts of different specific gravities
rubrics_metrics.description: The air contains parts that are in some places heavier and others lighter (as if different fluids) and when undisturbed they change places so the heavier becomes lowest and lighter uppermost, causing motions analogous to liquid stratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply familiar fluid statics (oil/water, heated fluids producing bubbles) to atmospheric parcels; expect layering and convective exchange where rarefaction/expansion creates lighter parcels that rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrestrial and celestial motions influence winds and regular breezes
rubrics_metrics.description: Earth's diurnal and annual motion, compounded with the moon's position and possible non-sphericity of the terraqueous globe, influence tides and winds and may explain regular breezes and trade-winds blowing frequently from a particular point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider compound motions (earth rotation, revolution, lunar effects) and global geometry as contributors to persistent wind patterns; this is offered as an adjunct to purely local thermodynamic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressed force/impetus can project vapours upward independent of specific gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: When things are in commotion, impressed force or impulse (e.g., jets of water, subterraneous eruptions, earthquakes) can propel fluids and vapours upward regardless of their specific gravity relative to surrounding air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish static/thermostatic causes (gravity/elasticity differences) from dynamic/mechanical causes; when strong impulses are present, they may dominate vapour ascent and wind genesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression vs heating: different effects on air's spring and intensive gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Compression increases the spring and intensively increases gravity (same weight in less room); heating strengthens spring by rarefying parts, which may diminish intensive gravity and allow expansion upward — causing different barometric and atmospheric effects depending on confinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In closed vessels heating makes air press stronger on the mercury (quicker rise), but in open air heating may allow the atmosphere to expand upward rather than increase downward pressure. Consider confinement when interpreting thermometer/barometer effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer reading artifacts: trapped particles and freezing-induced expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercury in tubes may contain lodged aerial (or watery) particles that, when heated, expand and make the quicksilver swell and stand higher without increasing weight; similarly freezing may expand such particles producing higher readings without implying greater external air pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting high barometer readings in hot or frosty weather, account for possible trapped gas or water particles in the mercury column rather than attributing all change to external atmospheric pressure.
